tone: Dry: nobody plays the joke or looks to camera. The gags are physical (a toe over the tape and snapped back, a banana held out like a permission slip), and the cut lands on the movement, never on a reaction.

Held: two locked-off positions (A18), never a reverse from the queue's side of the tape. A: lens at counter height, 40 cm from the dripper, framing her from mid-chest down with her head above frame and looking back past her hands to the doorway, soft 3 m behind. Focus stays on the dripper, so nothing beyond her hands is sharp, and at the release the queue arrives as hands and objects at her elbow. B: about 10 cm off the floor, 0.9 m from the tape on her side, beside a table leg, level, about 24 mm equivalent (vertical view about 74° in 9:16 and 4:5). In 9:16 the tape sits about 57% down and the ghost line about 63% down, and the frame top clears about 90 cm where the queue stands, so no child's face can enter; the toddler's feet dangle at the top edge. In 16:9, B holds ankles to knees. (Not 20 cm at 1.4 m: that framing puts a seven-year-old's face in the 9:16 frame.) The toe gag plays in B: the toe crosses and snaps back, and a grey sock steps in beside it. The hood hook itself is never shown.

Quiet: sound is the score: the tap into the kettle and its rising rumble, the hand grinder's crunch, the kettle's click, the hiss of the bloom, each drip. The queue's held noise stays small: a sock squeaking on the floor, the slip's paper, the toddler's heel tapping her father's hip. Music: none (A14). On the clack, the held noise returns all at once: feet, a chair scrape, a zip, a school bag dropped. No voices. If the drip isn't audible from the doorway (A16), the queue waits on the clack alone and the drip is heard only in A's close sound.
Not calm-amid-chaos: no noisy montage that falls silent when she pours, no slow-motion pour or drip, no sun across a spotless counter, no mug at a window, no voice-over about time for yourself.

brief.premise: School morning. Across the kitchen doorway runs a strip of blue painter's tape, scuffed grey in the middle where toes land, beside the pale ghost of an older line 40 cm nearer the counter. A mother of three fills the kettle; as its rumble rises, her daughter skids onto the tape in socks, permission slip and pen at arm's length. Nobody crosses. Nobody speaks. She sets her Solace dripper on the lopsided mug her eldest glazed, then grinds by hand; her son hops up in one shoe, its pair under the table on her side. The kettle clicks; the bloom hisses. Her partner joins the back, the toddler on his hip holding out an unpeeled banana like her big sister's slip. As she pours, the son's toe crosses the line and snaps back: his sister has hooked his hood, pen still in her fist. She never turns. The last drop falls; she lifts the dripper off and sets it down with a clack, and the queue crosses at once: without turning, she points under the table, and the slip, the shoe with its laces trailing and the banana reach her elbow while the full mug waits.

content.format_rationale: Ad spot (A2): one proposition paid off by one turn in 60 s. The queue builds behind the tape and the clack releases it. Runner-up: social series, one family member per episode. It lost because the payoff is accumulation, and episodes would make it a repeated gag with no release. Time compresses by the cut, never by speed. The clock starts when she fills the kettle, and each cut jumps one stage (heating, grinding, bloom, pour, drawdown, last drop) and adds one interruption. No dissolves, time-lapse or on-screen clock, and no super names a duration (A7). Route: AI-generated (A1), with the dripper matched to a reference not yet supplied (A5). Floor plan in A18. Make-or-break shot: B's tape frame reading as a house rule within 2 s on a phone. Week-1 tests at phone size: 4 generations each of B at 16:9 and 9:16, 4 of A's pour against the reference, and 4 of A's clack with the doorway emptying behind her. What it takes: 1 location (the kitchen and its doorway). 5 on-camera roles, 3 of them children. 0 voices. 0 lip-synced lines. 5 consistent characters held below the neck: her grey sweatshirt with the cuffs pushed up and a hair tie on her wrist, the daughter's grey school socks, the son's single untied navy trainer, the partner's brown felt slippers, the toddler's bare feet and banana. 26 new generated video shots (D01 14, D02 7, D03 5; D04 reuses D01), plus 3 stills. Product reference: not supplied (A5). Hand-and-product shots: 6 (D01 shots 2, 5, 7 and 11; D02/D03 shared shots 2 and 5), covering setting the dripper on the mug, the bloom, the pour, and the lift and clack. Hands with props: 2 (the grinder, D01-3; the signing, D02-7). Product alone: the drip in the crescent gap (D01-9, D02-4) and every end frame. Cost flags, each beside its beat. Children (the queue, every video): already the cheap version, since they are seen below the chin in B and soft in A, so there is no likeness to clear and no face to hold consistent. Hands and water (bloom and pour, D01-5, D01-7, D02/D03-2): fall back to a locked A frame on the spout and the dripper rim, one continuous pour, no hand adjustments. Hands on the grinder (D01-3): fall back to spooning pre-ground coffee from a tin (A20). Hands and paper (D02-7): the blank back of the slip, pen and hand only, no legible text. Alternative (not briefed): the same ten minutes at 5:40 a.m., before anyone is awake, ending when the first footsteps hit the stairs.

what_makes_it_specific: Source idea: "Solace makes a $38 ceramic pour-over dripper, glazed by hand, one cup at a time. The ten minutes of making coffee by hand are the only part of a parent's morning nobody interrupts."

Kept: "The ten minutes of making coffee by hand are the only part of a parent's morning nobody interrupts." The ten minutes run from filling the kettle to the last drop, the whole making, so the dripper is never given a brew time (A7).

Obvious version: a school-morning montage (spilled cereal, a lost shoe, a buzzing phone) that falls silent when she reaches the counter, with sunlit bloom close-ups, one private sip and a super about ten minutes that are yours.
Near-miss: the 'no talking until I've had my coffee' gag, a grumpy parent the family fears.

Differs by who and what it costs. Who: nobody fears her. The family keeps the rule for her behind a tape line (A3), each holding an interruption (a slip and pen, a sock-foot, a toddler's unpeeled banana), readable with the sound off and with no child's face. The chaos never goes quiet; it queues. Cost: each pays while waiting, and the clack opens the line before her first sip: the last drop hands the whole bill back to her.

Product role: the drip is the household's clock. The queue waits on the dripper, not on her (A16). The last drop ends the making, the lift and clack open the line, and the end frame sets the dripper beside the lopsided mug at the same scale and height, glaze to glaze, so 'Glazed by hand.' lands over two hand-glazed things. Swap in a machine-glazed cone and the rhyme breaks. Fallbacks, written in: if the drip isn't audible from the doorway, the queue waits on the clack alone and the drip is heard only in A's close sound. Glaze detail on the dripper comes only from the reference (A5); if the reference shows no visible hand variation, the super carries 'Glazed by hand.' alone and the mug rhyme stays compositional.

Added (A13): the lopsided mug her eldest glazed. The dripper rests on the rim's high points, and the low side leaves a crescent gap where we see the drip (A21; fallback: a thumb-sized notch in a level rim).

Added (A19): the ghost of an older tape line, 40 cm nearer the counter. The queue once stood closer, and she has since won the 40 cm back: the rule has been renegotiated once, in her favour. The art department lays both lines, and B holds both (tape about 57% down, ghost about 63% down in 9:16).

Added (A23): the toddler on her father's hip holds an unpeeled banana out at arm's length, copying her sister's slip. It replaces the obvious version's buzzing phone, reads with the sound off and needs no caption, and at the release it is one more thing handed back to her.
Taste note broken on purpose: the kettle, grinder and scale stay unbranded (no real brands). The tape, the ghost line, the mug and the banana carry the one real detail per setup.

story_seed.protagonist: A mother of three on a school morning, making coffee by hand with her back to the kitchen doorway.
story_seed.want: One cup, made by hand from filling the kettle to the last drop, without anyone needing her.
story_seed.obstacle: The whole morning is already at the door (a permission slip, a missing shoe, a toddler's unpeeled banana), held back only by a strip of tape.
story_seed.turn: The queue grows with every stage from the kettle to the pour, and a toe crosses the line and is hooked back by the hood, while she never turns.
story_seed.ending: The last drop falls; she lifts the dripper off and sets it down with a clack, and the queue crosses at once: without turning, she points under the table, and the slip, the shoe with its laces trailing and the banana reach her elbow while the full mug waits.

tone: Dry: nobody plays the joke or looks to camera. The gags are physical (a toe over the tape and snapped back, a banana held out like a permission slip), and the cut lands on the movement, never on a reaction.

Held: two locked-off positions (A18), never a reverse from the queue's side of the tape. A: lens at counter height, 40 cm from the dripper, framing her from mid-chest down with her head above frame and looking back past her hands to the doorway, soft 3 m behind. Focus stays on the dripper, so nothing beyond her hands is sharp, and at the release the queue arrives as hands and objects at her elbow. B: about 10 cm off the floor, 0.9 m from the tape on her side, beside a table leg, level, about 24 mm equivalent (vertical view about 74° in 9:16 and 4:5). In 9:16 the tape sits about 57% down and the ghost line about 63% down, and the frame top clears about 90 cm where the queue stands, so no child's face can enter; the toddler's feet dangle at the top edge. In 16:9, B holds ankles to knees. (Not 20 cm at 1.4 m: that framing puts a seven-year-old's face in the 9:16 frame.) The toe gag plays in B: the toe crosses and snaps back, and a grey sock steps in beside it. The hood hook itself is never shown.

Quiet: sound is the score: the tap into the kettle and its rising rumble, the hand grinder's crunch, the kettle's click, the hiss of the bloom, each drip. The queue's held noise stays small: a sock squeaking on the floor, the slip's paper, the toddler's heel tapping her father's hip. Music: none (A14). On the clack, the held noise returns all at once: feet, a chair scrape, a zip, a school bag dropped. No voices. If the drip isn't audible from the doorway (A16), the queue waits on the clack alone and the drip is heard only in A's close sound.
Not calm-amid-chaos: no noisy montage that falls silent when she pours, no slow-motion pour or drip, no sun across a spotless counter, no mug at a window, no voice-over about time for yourself.

normalized_brief.logline: For the ten minutes she makes coffee by hand, nobody interrupts a mother of three: her family queues behind a tape line until her Solace dripper's last drop, then crosses before her first sip.
normalized_brief.premise: School morning. Across the kitchen doorway runs a strip of blue painter's tape, scuffed grey in the middle where toes land, beside the pale ghost of an older line 40 cm nearer the counter. A mother of three fills the kettle; as its rumble rises, her daughter skids onto the tape in socks, permission slip and pen at arm's length. Nobody crosses. Nobody speaks. She sets her Solace dripper on the lopsided mug her eldest glazed, then grinds by hand; her son hops up in one shoe, its pair under the table on her side. The kettle clicks; the bloom hisses. Her partner joins the back, the toddler on his hip holding out an unpeeled banana like her big sister's slip. As she pours, the son's toe crosses the line and snaps back: his sister has hooked his hood, pen still in her fist. She never turns. The last drop falls; she lifts the dripper off and sets it down with a clack, and the queue crosses at once: without turning, she points under the table, and the slip, the shoe with its laces trailing and the banana reach her elbow while the full mug waits.

content.audience_tension: Who: parents who make coffee by hand on school mornings (kettle, hand grinder, a dripper or another hand brewer). They stand at the counter with their back to the kitchen doorway while the morning's asks arrive before the school run: a slip to sign, a shoe to find, a banana to peel. They buy a new dripper when the old one chips or cracks, or when someone gives them one (H8, a guess). The media proxy is in assumptions (S2). In their voice: I'd never tell my kids to wait for me, yet the few minutes at the counter when nobody needs me are the ones I'd hate to give up. [H1, a guess, not a verbatim] The pull: being the parent who is always available, against guarding one stretch where they aren't needed. What they'd hate to admit: that they want the family to wait. Asking why once past 'time', the loss isn't minutes; it's the one part of the morning when they are nobody's next task. Take the product away and it still holds: this is about a parent and a family, not coffee gear. The scene it gives the CD: her back to a doorway where the whole morning is already standing, and at their feet the ghost of an older line 40 cm nearer the counter (A19). The queue once stood closer, and she has won that ground back: the wish they'd hate to admit, laid down in tape.
content.desired_behavior: Goal: new buyers order the $38 dripper (F1) on Solace's own site, so each order books $38 there (A8: own-site cart, unconfirmed; S10). New buyers means parents who already make coffee by hand and don't own a Solace dripper. Existing Solace owners are not the target: the facts name one product and no repeat purchase. From: brewing by hand on whatever brewer is already on the counter, and buying another only when it chips or cracks, or when one arrives as a gift (H8). Before that, nothing gives them a reason to look at another one. To: orders the $38 dripper on the Solace product page after clicking through from D02 'The slip'. D03 runs split against it on orders per 1,000 impressions, and budget follows the better cut. Why D02 carries the To and D03 doesn't: the slip is signed flat on the counter beside the dripper, so the product sits inside the payoff action, while D03's trainer is held out at her elbow, next to the product but not part of what she does with it. content.product_relevance: Moment (the film's): a school morning at the kitchen counter, her back to the doorway, from filling the kettle to the last drop. She makes her cup by hand while the morning's asks line up behind the tape. Why the moment needs a hand brewer at all: a machine or a pod makes the cup by itself, so a parent standing beside one is free. She is free, so she is asked (category knowledge, H5). A pour-over is poured by hand and ends on a last drop (H5), so the morning has something to wait on and a point where it is released. What goes wrong without Solace's dripper: for this audience, nothing goes wrong in the brewing. Their brewer already makes the cup by hand and already holds them at the counter (A4). What the end frame shows instead: the mug underneath is the lopsided one her eldest glazed (premise, A13), and the dripper on it is a 'ceramic pour-over dripper' (F1), 'glazed by hand' (F2): glaze to glaze. Whether the brewer they own was glazed by hand is unknown (H2, H3). Blocked: needs a verified fact that the Solace dripper does something in the pour that the brewer they own does not. Until Solace supplies one, the work claims no functional advantage. Product role: the dripper, not her mood, decides when the morning's turn comes (development: 'the drip is the household's clock'; whether the drip is audible from the doorway is A16). That keeps out the near-miss of a parent the family fears: nobody is waiting on her temper. It holds with no logo and no price: a last drop through a dripper glazed by hand, beside a mug her eldest glazed, needs neither the name nor the $38. Barrier: this audience already has a working hand brewer on the counter, so nothing tells them they need another, and $38 is money spent on themselves on a family morning (H2; H7 is rejected as the tension but still stands as a barrier). Does the proposition get past it? Partly. F2 gives people who care how a thing is made a reason to choose this dripper when the old one chips or has to be replaced (H8). It gives no reason to replace a brewer that works. It gets past the Barrier for that group (H2) and for a partner buying it as a gift (H2 flight read), but not for someone who buys on function; that would need the blocked fact above. Permission: 'glazed by hand' (F2) is something a viewer could check on the object, but only if the product reference shows hand variation in the glaze (A5, not supplied). Until then: not established.
content.single_minded_proposition: The morning queues until the last drop leaves ceramic glazed by hand. (Replaces key_message: no F# supports its duration, 'ten minutes' (A7), or its superlative, 'only'.)
proof_points: [F1] Supports "last drop": "Solace makes a $38 ceramic pour-over dripper". 'Pour-over dripper' is the fact's own wording: water is poured over and the cup comes through drop by drop, so the making ends on a drop. That the drawdown ends on a clean last drop is category knowledge (H5), and the proposition is contingent on it (S3). The proposition says when the drops stop. It says nothing about how long, how well or how much (A7).

[F2, with F1] Supports "ceramic glazed by hand": "glazed by hand" [F2], on "Solace makes a $38 ceramic pour-over dripper" [F1]. F1 supplies the word 'ceramic', which is the whole of the material claim (must_avoid: no material claim beyond 'ceramic'). This proof separates Solace's dripper from the brewer already on the counter (Barrier, H2), and it is the line on D01's end card, 'Glazed by hand.' Whether the glazing by hand can be seen on screen depends on the product reference (A5).
success_criteria: Metric (the To, as a rate): Solace dripper orders per 1,000 impressions, click-attributed, reported separately for D01 (pre-roll), D02 (the named To), D03 and D06, with a UTM per deliverable. D01's product-page source is kept apart. Its event is a tap (tap-to-play or tap-to-unmute in the gallery, S8), never the page load, and it is read as orders per 1,000 product-page sessions with a D01 tap. People who tap choose to, so their rate shows whether D01 earns its gallery slot, not what it adds; if the site can split traffic, sessions whose gallery includes D01 against sessions without it give the lift. Target: above Solace's current rate for the same placements (the direction comes from the client's objective; the baseline number is for the client to supply). hypotheses: H2 Riskiest (the barrier, and the proposition's second half): most of this audience already has a working hand brewer on the counter, and the reason they'd order Solace's is that it is 'glazed by hand' (F2), not what it does. Why it outranks H1: H1 decides whether the film lands; H2 decides whether anyone orders, and the objective is orders. Test (pre-launch, unprompted): in the same eight interviews as H1, after the H1 section and before the dripper or the price appears, ask 'Tell me about the last brewer you bought: what made you choose that one?' After that, and not before, show the dripper and the $38 and ask what would make them order another. The interview order, H1 section first, is kept, so the cost doesn't change. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist, with Solace. Kills it if: fewer than 3 of 8 raise how the brewer was made, or who made it, without being asked. Then the proposition doesn't get past the Barrier, and the work needs the functional fact in blockers. Flight read (after launch, not a kill): a two-question survey on Solace's order confirmation, 'What did you brew with before this?' and 'Did you buy this for yourself or as a gift?' If most buyers came from machines or pods, the audience is people new to pour-over, not switchers, and the Barrier line changes. If most are gifts, the buyer is a partner, not the parent at the counter: that gets around H7's spending-on-themselves barrier and changes the Who.

H1 (the tension): parents who brew by hand on school mornings hold both of these: they'd never ask the family to wait, and making the cup is a stretch they guard because nobody needs them in it. They'd hate to admit the second out loud. In their voice: I'd never tell my kids to wait for me, yet the few minutes at the counter when nobody needs me are the ones I'd hate to give up. Test: eight 20-minute interviews with parents who brew by hand on school mornings, opening with 'walk me through yesterday morning, from getting up to the school run', with no mention of coffee or interruptions until the end. Two people score the transcripts separately. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist. Kills it if: fewer than 4 of 8 single out the coffee-making, unprompted, as a stretch they keep for themselves or are left alone in. The second half (what they'd hate to admit) is killed separately if fewer than 2 of those who single it out hedge or apologise for wanting it without being asked (calling it selfish, laughing it off, asking that the kids not hear). Then the tension has no second half, and the proposition becomes a benefit, not a permission.

H8 (the buying moment, in Who and From): people who brew by hand buy a new dripper when the old one chips, cracks or breaks, or when someone gives them one, not while the one they have still works. Test: H2's last-brewer question in the same eight interviews, followed only by 'And what happened to the one before it?' Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist. Kills it if: fewer than 3 of 8 describe a chip, crack or break, or a gift, as how their current brewer came to be on the counter. Then they buy while the old one still works, the From drops its 'only when', and the flight read carries more of the effect than the 90-day read.

H5 (category knowledge; the proposition is contingent on it, S3): a pour-over dripper is poured by hand from the kettle, and its drawdown ends at a point you can see (the last drop, then the lift). Also category knowledge, used in product_relevance: a machine or a pod makes the cup by itself, so a parent standing beside one is free. Test: read Solace's own brewing instructions or product copy, or ask Solace; for the film, development's A16 check on whether the drip is audible from the doorway. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist, with Solace. Kills it if: Solace describes any use that isn't hand-poured, or the dripper has no clean end to its drawdown in real time. Then the proposition's 'last drop' becomes the lift, and the product-relevance moment ends on the lift and clack alone (development's A16 fallback).

H3 (rivals and category conventions): no rival leads its ads or product page with a parent's morning, or with 'glazed by hand' as the reason to buy. The rivals to check are the pour-over dripper brands Solace competes with, plus small-batch ceramic makers who also glaze by hand, since the proposition's distinctiveness rests on F2. Any of them could say the proposition. Conventions to look for in the audit, so the routes can break them on purpose (a guess about the category, not a finding): overhead bloom close-ups; slow-motion pours; a gooseneck kettle on a sunlit, spotless counter; grams, ratios or timers on screen; a lone first sip at a window. The film as written breaks four of them: the bloom is shot at counter height at real speed, not overhead; there is no slow motion; the counter carries a dish rack and a charging cable, with no sun flooding it; and there is no sip at all. The remaining break (grams, ratios or timers on screen) is only half in the film. Timers are out, since development allows no on-screen clock. Grams and ratios stay out only if any scale in frame shows no readout. That is a note sent to development and production design (blockers), not something the film already does. Test: review 30 days of each named rival's live ads in public ad libraries, plus its product page. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist (needs Solace's competitor list: blocker). Kills it if: any of them leads with a parent's morning or with 'glazed by hand' as the reason to buy. Then the fallback wording in assumptions (S5) applies.

H4 (the reading): viewers read the tape line as the family keeping a rule for her, not as a parent shutting children out or a family afraid of her (the near-miss). They read the ending, where the queue crosses before her first sip, as the deal working, not as her losing. Test: show D01's B tape frame and the clack-to-release at phone size, muted, to ten parents, and ask 'what's the rule here, who made it, and how did it end for her?' Owner: Creative Director, with the Brand and Audience Strategist. Kills it if: 3 or more of 10 read punishment, fear or neglect, or read the ending as her defeat.

H6 Rejected (tension draft 2, craft against speed). In their voice: I brew by hand because it tastes better, yet on school mornings I'm one bad week from a pod machine. Rejected: it's a time-and-convenience tension. Asked why once more, it becomes H1: what they'd lose isn't the taste but the stretch nobody needs them in. It also pulls the work toward speed and brew time, which A7 bars. Revive if: the H1 interviews show parents, unprompted, dropping hand brewing on school mornings for speed.

H7 Rejected (tension draft 3, spending on themselves). In their voice: I'll buy the kids' things without a second thought, yet anything just for me needs a reason. Rejected: it holds without the product, but it pushes the work into justifying $38, a value argument with no fact behind it, and away from the moment. It stays live as part of the Barrier. Revive if: add-to-carts from D02 and D03 hold at or above baseline while orders fall below it, and a checkout exit question names spending on themselves.

It stops short of 9 for two reasons. The buyable proxy is not on the page: "The media proxy is in assumptions (S2)", and the next departments receive only audience_tension and the proposition. And the proposition itself reads two ways: "until the last drop leaves ceramic glazed by hand".
evidence.distinctiveness: Some findings could only come from this idea. The ghost line becomes the tension made visible: "The queue once stood closer, and she has won that ground back: the wish they'd hate to admit, laid down in tape." The case for the category needs this particular film: "a machine or a pod makes the cup by itself, so a parent standing beside one is free. She is free, so she is asked". The To is chosen from the payoff itself: "the slip is signed flat on the counter beside the dripper, so the product sits inside the payoff action, while D03's trainer is held out at her elbow". What keeps it at 8 is the proposition's product half. The page admits it could transfer: "Any of them could say the proposition". Lucas's idea is clearest in the tension ("the one part of the morning when they are nobody's next task"). routes.central_idea: Behind the tape, the morning waits on a dripper glazed by hand, not on her.
routes.emotional_promise: The guilt-free relief of a clack, not a word from her, sending the whole queue over the tape at once.
routes.product_role: Job: the household's clock. The queue waits on the dripper, not on her. If the drip is audible from the doorway (A16), the row in B rocks forward on each drip and lifts its heels together on the longest gap. The last drop, the lift and the clack then open the line. Under the A16 fallback the queue waits on the clack alone. That is still the dripper's sound, not a word or a look from her, so the line stays true, and the last drop is held on screen 17 frames before the lift. The dripper is a tool first (set on the mug, bloomed, poured through, dripping) and becomes the hero only in the end frame. First appearance: D01 at 0:03 in A, in use on the lopsided mug (skippable 16:9, inside 5 s); D02/D03 at 0:02 (vertical, inside 3 s); D04 at 1.2 s on the proposed timing (1.5 s on development's); sharp in D05 and in D06 frame 2. Handling: she lifts it by the handle or flange the reference shows (A5) and sets it down flat, base ring to board: a firm contact, not a drop. No bare fingertips on a just-brewed cone (that would imply a heat claim) and no drop (that would imply a chip claim, and chipping is H8's replacement trigger). Brand assets and where they sit: the dripper's own form and glaze, taken from the reference only (A5), with no generated glaze detail. 'Solace. Glazed by hand.' over D01's end frame at 56-60 s, in the lower third at frame right, 66-78% down: above the skip button's corner and clear of the dripper and the mug. routes.product_role: Job: the present, and what its givers wait on. It comes out of kraft paper the children have scribbled on in red crayon, sealed with strips from the same roll of blue painter's tape that now runs, fresh, across the doorway. Last night the family pulled up the old line and laid a new one 40 cm further from the counter, so the tape, the 40 cm and the dripper read as one present. The partner, who bought it, stands first on the new tape and crosses last. He is the giver and nothing else: the sister's sock, not his slipper, keeps the line, as in the seed. The dripper is a tool first: on the mug at 3 s, bloomed, poured through, dripping. In the end frame it becomes the hero beside the other present on the counter, the lopsided mug her eldest glazed: two presents glazed by hand, one of them by a child. First appearance: D01 at 0:03 in A, already on the mug with the paper open beside it (skippable 16:9, inside 5 s); the unwrapping is heard over B, never seen. D02/D03 at 0:02 (vertical, inside 3 s); D04 at 1.2 s (proposed timing). Handling: lifted by the handle or flange the reference shows (A5) and set down flat, base ring to board: a firm contact, not a drop. Brand assets and where they sit: the dripper's form and glaze, from the reference only (A5). There is no Solace box or branded packaging: the present comes in the children's paper, so nothing generated carries the name. Supers as in R1: 'Solace. Glazed by hand.' at 56-60 s, lower third, frame right, above the skip button's corner; 'Solace' and '$38' at 18-20 s, 20-30% down, left of centre; sound captions at 58-64% down in A and 20-28% down in B; 'Solace' on D04, D05 and both D06 frames; '$38' on D06 frame 2. The paper's corner and its blue seal stay at the end frame's left edge, clear of the supers. Proof: 'Solace makes a $38 ceramic pour-over dripper'; 'glazed by hand'. Held back: 'one cup at a time' (A6). Implies nothing further: the paper is the family's, so there is no gift-box, gift-service or packaging claim. No price sits on the present, no super or caption sits beside the full mug, the drip or the pour, and there is no scale in frame. Rival test: a rival cone could come out of the same paper. routes.visual_language: Camera: A and B only (A18), locked-off, no reverse, on R1's 14-shot grid so the cost stays level. B's compositions centre on the brown felt slippers, with the queue building on either side of them and the ghost line pale 40 cm in front of his toes, where he stood yesterday. A is as in R1: 28 mm equivalent, lens 5 cm above a 90 cm counter, 40 cm from the dripper, 8° up in 16:9 and level in 9:16, focus fixed on the dripper's front rim at T4. The present's paper lies open at frame left at the dripper's distance, so it is as sharp as the dripper. R1's blocking holds. She (about 170 cm) pours upright, her head never forward of her hands. At the release the children and the partner stand beyond A's side edges (more than about 55 cm off her centre line in 16:9, about 30 cm in 9:16) or straight behind her torso: forearms and objects only. Any face, eye line, chin or mouth in frame rejects a take. B is as in R1: 24 mm, 10 cm off the floor, 0.9 m from the tape, level. In 9:16 the tape sits 57% down and the ghost line 63%, and the frame top clears about 90 cm. The toddler's bare feet dangle at the top edge in 9:16 and 4:5 only; 16:9 holds ankles to knees. Art department: the live line is fresh, sharp-edged, clean #3B7FC4 with no grey scuff (this changes development's 'scuffed grey in the middle'). The ghost line is the floor left paler where the old tape ran until last night, with a few specks of adhesive. Light: one key, overcast daylight through a glazed back door in the left side wall, frame left in both positions, about 6000K, low and soft, grazing the floor so the pale strip reads. The sink window behind A is the fill; 3:1. Colour, each an object in frame: #3B7FC4 the blue painter's tape, on the floor and on the present's seal; #C4A57A the kraft paper; #C8413B the children's red crayon on it; #7A5A3E the partner's brown felt slippers; #E6C84A the toddler's unpeeled banana. The dripper's glaze comes from the reference only (A5). Dressing: the dish rack's corner and a charging cable soft at A's edge; all unbranded; no scale in frame. Motion: real speed; time jumps only on the cut. Sound: source only, no music (A14). Under B's opening: the tap, the switch's click, the element's first tick, and, from the counter, the long rip of tape off paper as the slippers step on. Then, in A, the paper's crackle and the full rumble; the grinder; the kettle's click and the plastic click of its base (the board takes one set-down only, the dripper's); the bloom's hiss and each drip. On the clack the children's held noise returns at once; the slippers' scuff comes a beat later, alone. No voices.
routes.execution_example: BRAVE. Costs the belief that a present is paid for once, at the till: its givers pay for this one every morning, 40 cm further back. Keeps: the uninterrupted making from the kettle to the last drop, the tape and its ghost line, the queue growing stage by stage, the toe over the line and the sister's sock stepping in, the clack, the point under the table, the objects at her elbow and the full mug. Changes (yes/no questions for Lucas, in assumptions): this is the dripper's first morning, a present from the family. The ghost line is where the tape ran until last night, and the live line is fresh and unscuffed. The partner is first on the tape and last across. The unwrapping is heard, not seen. His hand takes the banana back. The present's paper stays at the end frame's edge. D03 is proposed as 'The present'. The Who widens to the partner who buys it (H2 flight read). Casting: a mother because the seed names one (A11). Here the partner is the giver, and he takes one ask back at the end, so the work is visibly shared. A11's swap plays every beat unchanged. Flagged for claims review (UK CAP/BCAP). Look: R1's two locked positions (A: 28 mm at T4, lens 5 cm above a 90 cm counter; B: 24 mm, 10 cm off the floor), with B centred on the slippers; overcast back-door key frame left, 6000K, 3:1; fresh tape #3B7FC4, kraft #C4A57A, red crayon #C8413B, slippers #7A5A3E, banana #E6C84A; no scale; source sound with the rip and the paper's crackle, no music. Tags: G generated from text; R from the reference pending (A5); C composite; no P beats (A1, no shoot budget). Every A beat carries R and waits for A5. If there is no reference by the end of week 1, the A tests slip and Lucas is told. D01, 60 s, 16:9: 0-3 s [G] B: the fresh blue tape, sharp-edged, and the pale ghost line 40 cm nearer. 0-1.2 s, the tap runs into the kettle; at 1.3 s the switch clicks, then the element's tick. At 1.5 s brown felt slippers step onto the tape at centre frame and stop, the giver first on the line, as the long rip of tape off paper comes from the counter. 3-7 s [R+G+C, with the crayon marks composited from a studio drawing so no generated scribble can turn into letters; fallback R+C: no hands, the dripper on the mug, the paper open beside it, the last strip already off] A: at 3.0 s the dripper is already on the lopsided mug, with the scribbled kraft paper open at frame left, and one hand peels the last strip of blue tape off its fold. The paper crackles; the rumble comes in full. In the doorway, one tall soft shape holds a yellow banana out from its hip. 7-11 s [R+G; fallback R+G: spooning pre-ground coffee from a tin (A20)] A: the grinder's crunch; a smaller grey-and-white shape skids into the soft doorway, slip held out. 11-14 s [G] B: heather-grey socks settle on the tape beside the slippers, toes curled over its counter-side edge. 14-20 s [R+G; fallback R: locked on the spout and rim, no hands] A: the kettle clicks off; the bloom pour; the grounds hiss; the kettle goes back on its base with a plastic click; a small figure hops into the soft doorway. 20-23 s [G] B: a sock-foot and one untied navy trainer land on the slippers' other side; its pair lies under the table edge at frame left. 23-30 s [R+G; fallback R: spout and rim only; last resort C: a G stream over an R dripper plate] A: she pours upright, one continuous pour at real speed; the red scribbles sit at frame left. 30-34 s [G] B: the sock-foot's toe crosses the tape and snaps back; a heather-grey sock steps in beside it. The slippers don't move. The hood hook is never shown. 34-40 s [R+G; fallback R+C: G drops over an R still plate; mug fallback: a notch in a level rim (A21)] A: the drip in the crescent gap, facing the lens, slowing. 40-44 s [G] B: the children's feet fidget on either side; the slippers stay still, 40 cm behind the pale strip. 44-48 s [R+G; fallback C: R product plate over a G soft-doorway plate] A: the last drop at 46.1 s holds 17 frames before the lift at 46.8 s. She lifts the dripper by the handle or flange (A5) and at 47.6 s sets it down flat, base ring to board. Clack, and the soft doorway begins emptying forward. Cut at 48.0 s, 10 frames after the clack. 48-51 s [G] B: the socks and the sock-foot cross at once, picked up mid-stride; the slippers hold the tape one beat, alone, then cross. 51-55 s [R+G; fallback C: G hand-and-object plates keyed in at her elbow over an R dripper-and-mug plate; if hands fail, the slip and the trainer's laces alone] A: without turning, she points under the table. The slip, the trainer with its laces trailing and the banana reach her elbow on forearms from beyond the frame's side edges, and a larger hand in a brown cuff takes the banana back. 55-60 s [R+G+C; fallback R+C: open after she has gone] A: the dripper, still wet, beside the full lopsided mug: two presents glazed by hand, glaze to glaze. content.recommendation_rationale: Rationale: R1 plays the proposition, 'The morning queues until the last drop leaves ceramic glazed by hand', in one beat: D01 44-48 s, the last drop held 17 frames, the lift, the clack, the doorway lurching forward. The dripper, not her, sets the release (H4); R2 needs H1's admission and R3 needs gift buyers. D02 'The slip' serves 'the share of viewers who can say, unprompted, what the child wanted and when they got it', then 'Solace dripper orders per 1,000 impressions, click-attributed' (criteria 5, 1). Gives up: the admission as the film's spine. In R2 the family keeps her pause down to the tape: the toe hauled off the old line, the tape pressed flat, the lace drawn back, the kettle's thump ignored. In R1 the ghost line is dressing that rewards a second look. R1 also gives up the giver as buyer (R3's slippers first on fresh tape, the 40 cm and the dripper as one present) and a new structure: R1 is the development's film as written, plus the heel lift. Failure (1, the idea's): the last drop at phone size, in D02 9-14 s and D01 44-48 s. At 0.4 m on 28 mm, a 4 mm drop is about 14-16 px wide on a 1080-wide 9:16 screen, inside a crescent gap against dark coffee, and both R1's line and kill test (b) rest on it. Fix: the gap faces the lens at frame centre, and the 6000K key from frame left puts a highlight on the drop against the mug's shadowed inside. Run four week-1 generations of the drip at 9:16 on a grey placeholder cone, judged on a phone (a legibility test, never cut in), and repeat them on the reference when A5 lands. Fallback: the A21 notch. Failure (2): D02 0-1.0 s, B at phone size. The tape can read as a floor stripe before the socks stop on it, and grey socks can vanish into a grey scuff. Fix: the socks enter at 0 s and stop dead by 1.0 s, toes curled over the tape's counter-side edge. The socks are light heather #C4C6C8, the scuff is worn dark blue-grey (about #6E7C8E) on #3B7FC4 tape over #8F6B47 oak, and the ghost line stays pale but in frame at 63%. Run four week-1 generations at 9:16 before any other B shot. Kill test: show the first muted cut (week-1 B plates with boarded A frames, or the first generations once A5 lands) at phone size to 10 parents and ask what let the queue cross. The idea has failed if (a) 3 or more of 10 read fear, punishment or neglect (H4), or (b) 3 or more of 10 answers are coded Fail. Coding frame: a Pass names the coffee finishing, the dripper coming off, or the sound. A Fail names her permission or a signal from her ('when mum was ready', 'she let them'). Two coders score separately, and a disagreement counts as a Fail. An answer that names neither is coded None and doesn't count toward the kill; 3 or more None sends the drop back to Failure (1), a craft fix. Either kill means the dripper has not taken the rule off her: switch to R2, where the family owns the rule and nothing hangs on the drip. Under A16's fallback the line stays true, since the queue waits on the dripper's clack, not on her. The 17-frame hold (last drop 46.1 s, lift 46.8 s, set-down 47.6 s, cut 48.0 s) keeps the drop on screen for (b). Case R2-stretch-ghost-line: strategy.hypotheses H1, second half, at a studio threshold above its survival line (H1 survives at 2 hedgers among those who single the coffee-making out). If 4 or more of all 8 interviewees hedge or apologise for wanting it, unprompted, R2 is the pick. Only the family's keeping answers the admission, so she never has to ask. R2 is also the safer build if development's A16 check finds the drip inaudible from the doorway, since its queue never listens for it. Case R3-brave-the-present: strategy.hypotheses H8 and the H2 flight read. R3 is the pick, at launch or for the next flight, if 4 or more of the 8 interviewees say, unprompted, that the brewer on their counter was a gift (a studio threshold, above H8's kill line of 3 for chip-or-gift combined). It is also the pick if the order-confirmation survey shows most orders are gifts ('the buyer is a partner'). Only R3 speaks to the giver, and with D03 retold as 'The present', the split tests that buyer directly. Conventions (H3's list, a guess, not an audit; listed first in assumptions): (1) an overhead bloom close-up with a slow-motion pour; (2) a gooseneck kettle on a sunlit, spotless counter, with grams and a timer on screen; (3) the lone first sip at a window. R1 breaks all three: the bloom at counter height and real speed; overcast light on a counter with a dish rack and a cable, and no scale at all; no sip, with the mug full to the end. R2 turns (1) into its false ending, heard from the floor. R3 swaps (3)'s lone sip for its givers queueing, first on and last across. The ten one-liners, and why seven were killed, are in assumptions.

assumptions: The category's three most familiar ads (strategy H3's convention list: a guess about the category, not an audit; no rival ads were reviewed in this run): (1) the overhead bloom close-up with a slow-motion pour; (2) a gooseneck kettle on a sunlit, spotless counter, with grams, a ratio and a timer on screen; (3) the lone first sip at a window. All three routes break all three. All three also avoid the near-miss from outside the category, 'no talking until I've had my coffee'.

Ten one-liners drafted; the three furthest apart kept. (1) KEPT, R1: 'Behind the tape, the morning waits on a dripper glazed by hand, not on her.' (2) KEPT, R2: 'Her pause isn't taken from the family; they keep it for her, down to the tape.' (3) KEPT, R3: 'Her family's present: a dripper glazed by hand, and their queue moved 40 cm further back.' (4) KILLED, 'Ten minutes that are yours': a duration claim (A7) and the obvious version. (5) KILLED, 'No talking until I've had my coffee': the near-miss, a parent the family fears. (6) KILLED, 'The only coffee that makes the family wait': true of any pour-over, so any rival could headline it, and it is a comparison (must-avoid). (7) KILLED, 'The queue is how they love her': it costs nothing, since every parent already believes it, and it is sentimental (taste: dry over sentimental). (8) KILLED, 'Glazed by hand, like the mug her eldest made': the end frame's rhyme, not an idea, and it rests entirely on A5. (9) KILLED, 'The same ten minutes at 5:40 a.m., before anyone is up' (development's unbriefed alternative): no queue and no tape, so it drops Lucas's seed and drifts toward calm-amid-chaos. (10) KILLED, 'The 40 cm she won back', the ghost line's history told across years of mornings: it needs a multi-morning structure the seed doesn't have, and its best beat lives in R2 (the old ground) and R3 (the line moved as a present).

The row is reading the drip as the clock and is a beat early, which is dry and keeps the dripper, not her, in charge.

Reconciled notes (2), the week-1 drip test against the A5 hold: the notes ask both that every A beat wait for A5 and for four week-1 drip generations. Frame counts at 23.976 fps: 0.7 s = 17 frames, 0.6 s = 14 frames, 0.4 s = 10 frames. D02's 12.2-12.8 s hold is 14 frames (relabelled from '12-frame'). R2's D01 hold is 14 frames. All holds are above the 12-frame floor.

Claims: only F1 ('Solace makes a $38 ceramic pour-over dripper') and F2 ('glazed by hand') are stated. F3 ('one cup at a time') is held back pending A6. No functional advantage is claimed (the strategy's blocked fact), and nothing ties 'ten minutes' to the brew or the dripper (A7). That a pour-over's drawdown ends on a visible last drop is category knowledge (H5), not a Solace claim.

Super and caption placement: D01's 'Solace. Glazed by hand.' in the lower third, frame right, at 66-78% down, assumes the skip button sits in the bottom-right corner below that band. In 9:16, sound captions sit at 58-64% down in A and 20-28% down in B, which keeps the tape (57%) and the ghost line (63%) clear. Confirm both against each platform's safe zones.

Pairing fixes applied: R2's central idea and product job are rewritten so only the family's keeping plays them, with the false ending kept as a supporting beat. In R3, 'the line's keeper' is cut: the partner is only the giver, and the sister's sock steps in beside the toe, as in the seed.

Taste notes followed: restraint (no voice-over, and captions name sounds only), hands before faces (no face anywhere), sound design before music (no music), dry over sentimental, the product a tool before a hero, and one real detail per setup (the ghost line, the lopsided mug, the banana; R3 adds the children's paper). R1's pick rests on H4 (the tape reads as a rule kept for her, not a punishment) and H5 (a clean, visible last drop). Both are untested hypotheses, and kill test (a) and Failure (1) test them first.

evidence.specificity: A crew could shoot R1's D01 from this page. "a child at her elbow is about 0.8 m from the lens, where the blur drops to about 14 px on a face about 300 px tall. So the children and the partner stand beyond A's side edges (more than about 55 cm off her centre line in 16:9, about 30 cm in 9:16)". I rechecked the maths and it holds. At 24 mm, 10 cm up and 0.9 m back, the tape sits about 57% down and the ghost line about 63%. The 16:9 A frame tops out about 26 cm above the counter at the dripper and about 42 cm at her. The release is timed to the frame: "The last drop falls at 46.1 s and holds on screen 17 frames. The lift begins at 46.8 s ... At 47.6 s she sets it down flat ... Cut at 48.0 s, 10 frames after the clack." Supers, captions, five hex colours (each an object), the key light (source, direction, Kelvin, ratio) and the sound list are all placed. evidence.distinctiveness: The package could only belong to this brief. R2 has its sound grammar: "The kettle is a heavy, dull thump ... The dripper is a short, dry ceramic tock with no slosh. They are captioned '[knock]' and '[clack]'". R3 wraps the present in "strips from the same roll of blue painter's tape that now runs, fresh, across the doorway". R1 has the heel lift "on a gap longer than any before". But the craft brief's product test fails by the routes' own admission. R1 says "Rival test: a rival cone would make the same clack." R2 says "a rival cone could sit on the same board." R3 says "a rival cone comes out of the same paper just as well." Each route rests its difference on A5, which has not arrived. None uses the verified word 'ceramic' in the sound that releases the queue, although R2 already writes a "dry ceramic tock". R2's central idea, "Her pause isn't taken from the family; they keep it for her, down to the tape.", has no product and no proof, so any brand could run it. evidence.fit: Lucas's idea is recognisable in all three routes and sharper in R1: the morning waits on the dripper, not on her. Only F1 and F2 are stated as fact, with "Held back: 'one cup at a time' (A6)". The must-includes and must-avoids are handled line by line. The dripper appears by 3 s in the verticals and by 5 s in 16:9. Captions are bracketed sound descriptions. There is no scale readout, no face, no sip and no music. Supers are placed against the UI zones: "'Solace' and '$38' over the D02/D03 end frame at 18-20 s, left of centre, 20-30% down ... clear of the top 14%, the bottom 25-35% and the right 12%". The recommendation quotes the proposition, a beat, a success criterion and a cut, then gives "Gives up:", "Failure:", "Kill test:" and two "Case:" lines, each tied to a brief field (H1; H8 and the H2 flight read). It misses three craft-brief rules. (1) The category conventions are required first, but they come last and are referred to as "listed first in assumptions", which is not on the page. (2) The ten one-liners are not shown. (3) R2's central idea shows no verified proof point. Two must-include slips: D02 captions '[kettle rumbling]' before any rumble exists, and D04's A16 fallback puts '[drip]' at 1.2 s, ahead of the drop at 1.3 s. That breaks "every payoff reads with the sound off before the caption lands".
evidence.craft:
The technique is senior. The lens, blocking and blur figures are correct, and the page draws the right conclusion from them: "Tilting down does not fix it: at 4° down the dripper's top sits about 10% down, inside the top-14% UI zone." Claims hygiene reaches into the handling: "No bare fingertips on a just-brewed cone (that would imply a heat claim) and no drop (that would imply a chip claim, and chipping is H8's replacement trigger)." Every risky beat has a first try and a fallback. "Every A frame holds the dripper sharp, so every A beat carries R, and none generates until A5 arrives." A senior reviewer would still catch these on first read:
- D04's shortest cut puts the turn's key beat two frames after a cut from B to A ("1.2-3.2 s A, last drop at 1.3 s").
- D02's opening can't happen at real speed: "The tap runs to 0.7 s, the switch clicks at 0.8 s, and '[kettle rumbling]' lands on the element's first tick at 0.9 s."
- A falling drop cannot "hold on screen 17 frames".
- From a lens 5 cm above the counter, the gap shows only the bead forming at the outlet, not the drop falling.
- In R3 she peels the wrapping's last strip after the dripper is already on the mug.
- Kill test (a) switches to R2 on the fear/neglect reading. That reading comes from the tape line all three routes share, so R2 would not fix it.
- "The dripper, not her, sets the release (H4)" cites the wrong hypothesis.
